newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Syfrets reaps property division benefits. [CORRECTED 15:03 GMT]
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Syfrets reaps property division benefits. [CORRECTED 15:03 GMT]

text.p: South African investment management company Syfrets increased net income after tax by 32 percent for the year ended September 30 thanks to a solid performance by its property finance arm.
Group CEO Christopher Beatty told a news briefing the company's property finance operations continued to be a major contributor to profits for the second year running.
"The group's combined Syfrets Bank and Participation Bond advances book reached five billion rand during the year compared to 4.1 billion rand at the end of September last year," Beatty said.
Another division, Syfrets Property Finance, was now a leader in the commercial and industrial property finance market.

Net income before expenses (corrects by adding dropped phrase before expenses) for the group, which is a subsidiary of banking giant Nedcor Ltd, rose 32 percent to 100.8 million rand from 76.6 million a year ago.
In line with other financial institutions the group had experienced a tightening of margins, with a 23 percent growth in net interest income against a 29 percent growth in advances.
While it had been a disappointing year for the investment management division, inflows into the group's seven unit trusts remained comparatively stable at one billion rand, Beatty said.
"A new asset management process in April resulted in a dramatic improvement in institutional fund performance by year end," he said.

The group was involved in a major re-engineering process this year -- part and parcel of the growing international trend -- which focused on the re-design of the company's approach to the private investment market.
"Based on international benchmarks of best practice, Syfrets has set challenging new operational and financial targets for this core business area," Beatty said.
He predicted further growth in market share and profits in 1997 and said the group now had the capacity to significantly increase revenue.
"We are not seeking to cut costs but to significantly grow the revenue base with a comparatively slow increase in the cost base," Beatty added.
